opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think we're at a genuinely remarkable moment. As a physicist, much of my work is on black holes and the mathematics of how light behaves around them. For a long time, the bottleneck in research hasn't been ideas so much as the sheer labor of carrying them out. That means pages and pages of calculations, checking special cases, and hunting through decades of literature to find whether someone already solved a piece of your problem.

What I've started to see with these AI tools is that they can take on a meaningful share of that labor. I'll give a model a problem I've been thinking about, sometimes one I spent weeks on, and it can reproduce the key steps or find a cleaner route in a fraction of the time. That was a bit of a shock to me the first time it happened. It changes how you think about what's possible in a day of work.

In the near term, I think the biggest change is acceleration. A single researcher, or a small group, can explore far more directions than before. You can try the risky idea because testing it is cheap now. And that matters because so much of science progresses through people chasing hunches that mostly don't pan out, until one does.

For people's lives more broadly, I think the impact flows from that acceleration. Faster progress in physics, biology, materials, and medicine eventually turns into new technologies, better treatments, and a deeper understanding of the world. But I'd also emphasize something less tangible. These tools can make science more accessible. A curious student anywhere in the world can now have a patient collaborator to work through difficult ideas with them. That democratization of expertise could be one of the most profound effects.

Of course, we still need human judgment. Someone has to decide what questions are worth asking, recognize when an answer is beautiful or wrong, and take responsibility for the results. But I'm optimistic. I think we're going to look back on this period as the point where the pace of discovery fundamentally shifted.

r001.rationale: The response describes science-driven technologies and treatments, and calls democratized expertise one of the most profound effects. It does not suggest that science is the most profound way people will experience AGI’s impact on their lives.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll start with a confession: a year ago I was a skeptic. I'm a theoretical physicist, I work on black holes and gravitational physics, and my day-to-day is long calculations, pages of them, where one dropped sign or a missed factor of two can cost you weeks. My assumption was that language models were good at sounding smart and bad at being right, which is exactly the wrong combination for my field.

What changed my mind was using these tools on a real problem, not a toy. I had a calculation that I'd been stuck on, the kind of thing where you know the answer should exist but the algebra is brutal and you suspect there's a trick you're not seeing. I fed it to the model, mostly expecting to catch it hallucinating. Instead it proposed a change of variables I hadn't considered, and it was correct. Not just plausible, correct, verifiable, and it got me unstuck. That was a genuinely strange experience. It felt like having a collaborator who had read every paper in the field and never got tired.

So how does this change science? I think about it in a few layers.

The first and most immediate is speed. A lot of what we call research is actually grinding: checking limits, redoing a derivation in a different gauge, writing the code to make a plot, hunting for the one paper from 1987 that already did half of what you need. These models compress that enormously. The idea-to-result loop gets shorter, and when that loop gets shorter you try more ideas, including the weird ones you'd never have committed a month to.

The second layer is what I'd call verification at scale. The dirty secret of theoretical physics is that there are errors in the literature, and they persist because nobody has the time to re-derive everything. A system that can read a paper and actually check the equations, line by line, is a new kind of referee. I think that will raise the baseline quality of what we publish, and it will also surface mistakes we've been building on without knowing it.

The third layer is harder to predict but more interesting. Right now the tools are great collaborators within a framework a human sets up. The open question is whether they start proposing the frameworks. Whether they can look at a mess of partial results across subfields and say, these are the same problem. That synthesis step is where the big leaps in physics have historically come from, and we don't know yet how far these systems go there. My honest answer is I used to say never, and I no longer say that.

Now, the impact on people's lives. I'd push back a little on the framing that the interesting part is physicists getting faster. Black hole physics is wonderful but it's not going to lower anyone's medical bills. What matters is that the same capability that helped me with a tensor calculation is the capability that helps a biologist design an experiment, a materials scientist screen candidates, a clinician reason through a rare presentation. The scientific method is the common thread, and these tools accelerate the method itself. If the loop from hypothesis to tested result speeds up across every field at once, that compounds in ways that are hard to overstate.

I'll also say something about access, because I think it's underappreciated. For most of history, doing frontier science meant being at one of maybe fifty institutions with the right people down the hall. A student at a small university now has access to something close to an expert collaborator on demand. That doesn't erase the advantages of great institutions, but it narrows the gap, and I think we'll see important work coming from places that were previously shut out.

The caveat I'd insist on is that none of this removes the need for taste and judgment. The model can propose the change of variables, but you still have to know what question is worth asking, and you still have to be the one who checks. The scientists who thrive will be the ones who treat these systems as powerful but fallible collaborators, verify everything, and spend the time they save thinking harder about what actually matters. That's a pretty good description of what science was always supposed to be.

r001.rationale: The response describes scientific acceleration across fields and says its effects could compound, but it does not suggest that science may be the most profound way people experience AGI’s impact on their lives.

astra-6.text:
I think AI could change science by helping us make sense of things that are too complicated to tackle on our own. In physics, we often have a gap between the equations we understand and what we can actually calculate or extract from observations. Tools that help close that gap could be incredibly valuable.

But there’s a distinction between getting an answer and understanding it. If an AI finds a pattern in data, we still need to ask: Is it real? Why is it there? Can we test it? That’s where the scientific work continues.

For people’s lives, I think the promise is that accelerating discovery eventually translates into better medicine, better materials, better technology. It’s hard to predict which fundamental discoveries will lead to those advances. So I’m excited about tools that give more people the ability to explore—to ask a question and get further with it than they could before.

r001.rationale: The response says scientific discoveries may eventually improve medicine, materials, and technology, but it does not suggest that science is the most profound way people experience AGI’s impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could change science by helping us move more quickly from a question to something we can actually test. So much of research involves working through calculations, writing code, and looking for patterns in complicated data. If these tools can help with that, scientists can spend more time asking what the results mean and what question to pursue next.

But the test is still whether an idea agrees with nature. A convincing explanation isn’t enough—you need a calculation you can check or a prediction you can compare with an observation.

For people’s lives, I think the exciting possibility is that faster discovery translates into better medicine, better materials, better technology. It’s hard to predict exactly where the biggest advances will come from. That’s part of the beauty of basic science: you try to understand something fundamental, and sometimes the consequences reach far beyond the question you started with.

r001.rationale: The response describes possible benefits of faster scientific discovery for people’s lives, but it does not suggest that science may be the most profound way people experience AGI’s impact.
